newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Red Cross reports "dramatic" N.Korea food ration.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross reports "dramatic" N.Korea food ration.

text.p: The global Red Cross organisation IFRC said on Tuesday food rations across North Korea had dropped to a level four times lower than was normally considered essential to maintain a healthy population.

The IFRC Under-Secretary General for Disaster Response, Margareta Wahlstrom, told a news conference there was no indication yet of famine but reduction of the ration to 100 grams (3.5 ounces) a day would weaken resistance to disease throughout the country.
"This (the ration) is quite a dramatic figure in a country where people are totally reliant on the public distribution system for their food," she said.
The new level had been set by the North Korean government in the capital, Pyongyang, earlier this month.

Wahlstrom told the news conference, launching an overall appeal for $200 million to finance world-wide relief programmes, that the IFRC saw 400 to 450 grams (15 ounces to 1 lb) of food per person a day as its target in relief operations.

The IFRC -- the Geneva-based International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies -- has been working with the North Korean Red Cross for two years to sustain tens of thousands of people hit by floods in 1995 and 1996.

Last week, the federation said the situation in the reclusive communist state, still formally at war with its much richer neighbour South Korea, was critical. Finance and other support from the international community was urgent, the IFRC said.

The floods left half a million people homeless out of a total of 23 million and hit hard at the entire economy by destroying rice fields, roads, factories and livestock and flooding mines, according to relief organisations.
The IFRC says 5.2 million people were directly affected by the 1995 floods and a further 3.3 million last year. Its programmes are aimed at supporting 139,000 of the worst hit.
Although earlier appeals for funds were largely met, a call the IFRC issued last September for $9.2 million from its member societies and governments has raised only $700,000.
Wahlstrom said the "political dimension" of North Korea's international position and the fact that it was seen by some as a "rogue regime" always made it difficult to raise resources.

"It is quite evident that an injection into the state system is needed," she told the news conference. "North Korea is not an agricultural country, and would not be self-sufficient in food if it were integrated into the international system."

South Korea, which had been sending food shipments to the North, suspended them after accusing Pyongyang of landing 22 commandos from a submarine last September. All but two of the group died during a subsequent manhunt.
Seoul's own Red Cross is due to send 300 tonnes of flour and 15,000 pairs of socks later this week in the first delivery since the incident, for which the North formally apologised.

The United States, which is trying to improve relations with the North and is discussing an exchange of low-level diplomatic missions, as well as Japan have contributed to earlier IFRC-sponsored shipments.

Last week, the U.S. grain giant Cargill held talks in Pyongyang on food barter trade, a company spokesman said. Earlier this month, Washington told Cargill it could supply up to two million tonnes of grain to the North.
